lessons.title: Introduction to Variables & Assignment
lessons.docSection: §3.1 Using Python as a Calculator — Assignment
intro: Read the official tutorial section below, then complete the practice objectives in the editor.

sections.heading: Using Python as a Calculator
paragraphs: Let's try some simple Python commands. The interpreter acts as a simple calculator: you can type an expression into it and it will write the value. Expression syntax is straightforward: the operators `+`, `-`, `*` and `/` can be used to perform arithmetic; parentheses `()` can be used for grouping.

sections.heading: Assignment with =
paragraphs: The equal sign (`=`) is used to assign a value to a variable. Afterwards, no result is displayed before the next interactive prompt:
If a variable is not "defined" (assigned a value), trying to use it will give you an error — a `NameError`.

sections.heading: Variable names
paragraphs: Names can be letters, digits, and underscores. A name cannot start with a digit. Assignment creates a reference from the name to the value — think of a variable as a label for a value in memory.

tasks.text: Use print() to show your variable (like the tutorial).

lessons.successMessage: You assigned a value and printed it — just like the official tutorial.

lessons.title: Numbers, Strings & Booleans
intro: The official tutorial introduces numeric types and text (strings). Read each subsection, try the examples, then build your own program.

sections.heading: Numbers (int and float)
paragraphs: The integer numbers (e.g. `2`, `4`, `20`) have type **int**, the ones with a fractional part (e.g. `5.0`, `1.6`) have type **float**.
Division (`/`) always returns a float. To do floor division and get an integer result you can use the `//` operator; to calculate the remainder you can use `%`:

sections.heading: Text (strings)
paragraphs: Python can manipulate text (type **str**, "strings") as well as numbers. They can be enclosed in single quotes (`'...'`) or double quotes (`"..."`) with the same result.
The `print()` function produces readable output — it omits the enclosing quotes and interprets escape characters like `\n` for newline:
sections.code:
'spam eggs'
"Paris rabbit got your back :)! Yay!"
print('First line.\nSecond line.')
sections.codeOutput:
spam eggs
Paris rabbit got your back :)! Yay!
First line.
Second line.

sections.heading: Booleans in practice
paragraphs: Python has built-in boolean values `True` and `False` (always capitalized). You will use them soon with `if` statements. For now, know that comparisons like `5 > 3` produce a boolean.

lessons.exampleCode:
age = 14
height = 1.62
name = "Chifundo"
is_student = True
print(age, name, is_student)

tasks.text: Print all three on separate lines.

lessons.successMessage: Great work! You used the core data types from the official tutorial.

questions.prompt: Which symbol assigns a value in Python?
questions.explanation: A single equals sign `=` assigns. `==` compares equality (PSF tutorial §4.2).
Decimal numbers are floats in Python.

questions.prompt: Which is a valid variable name?
questions.explanation: Names may use letters, digits, underscores; they cannot start with a digit.

chapters.description: PSF Tutorial §4 — More Control Flow Tools

lessons.title: Comparisons and Boolean Logic
intro: Before `if` statements, the tutorial shows how Python evaluates conditions using comparison operators — the same operators used in real programs.

sections.heading: Comparison operators
paragraphs: The standard comparison operators are written the same as in C: `<` (less than), `>` (greater than), `==` (equal to), `<=`, `>=`, and `!=` (not equal to).
In Python, zero is false; any non-zero integer value is true. The condition in a loop or `if` can also be a string or list — anything with a non-zero length is true, empty sequences are false.

sections.heading: Combining conditions
paragraphs: Use `and` when both conditions must be true, and `or` when either condition is enough. This is how you model real rules in code.
sections.code:
has_ticket = True
age = 16
can_enter = has_ticket and age >= 13
print(can_enter)

lessons.exampleCode:
has_ticket = True
age = 16
can_enter = has_ticket and age >= 13
print(can_enter)

tasks.text: Print the result of your comparison.

lessons.title: If, Elif, and Else Statements
intro: Perhaps the most well-known statement type is the **if** statement. Read the official example, then write your own branching program.

sections.heading: if … elif … else
paragraphs: There can be zero or more **elif** parts, and the **else** part is optional. The keyword `elif` is short for "else if", and is useful to avoid excessive indentation.
The body of each branch is **indented** — indentation is Python's way of grouping statements. Use four spaces per level (the style shown throughout the tutorial).

sections.heading: Indentation matters
paragraphs: Every line inside an `if`, `elif`, or `else` block must be indented by the same amount. If you forget indentation, Python raises an `IndentationError`.
Try changing the value of `score` in the editor example to see different branches run.
